description: Worker tuning: the flag that is live, then waiting, slots, pollers, Java internals, load delivered, server.

options.content: **Read top to bottom: it's the order you diagnose in.** Change ONE tuning value at a time (flip the flag), let k6 hold each step for several Workflow durations, and compare the step where schedule-to-start first rises. Swap markers show when a new Worker generation started. Rule out the server (bottom row) before tuning Workers. See `demo/lab/README.md` for the measured cases.

panels.title: 1 · Which tuning is live (the feature flag)
Tuning mode
panels.description:
The flag's mode on the Workers serving this queue: MANUAL, RESOURCE_BASED or SDK_DEFAULTS.

Exported by SwappableWorker (demo/lab/javaworker). Without the flag exported as a metric, 'did the change help?' is answered from memory: nothing on the board says which config was live when the latency moved.

More than one value at once means Workers on the same queue disagree, mid-rollout or because a pod never picked up the flag (a ConfigMap mounted with subPath never updates).

panels.title: Flag rejected (range)
panels.description:
Flag values refused by validation, or swaps that failed to start. The previous config KEPT running, by design: a Worker that falls back to SDK defaults after a typo looks healthy and runs a config nobody chose.

Non-zero means the config you think you shipped is NOT live. The Worker log has the reason (e.g. 0 means 'SDK default', not 'none'; RESOURCE_BASED on 1.29-1.32 refused for the tuner hang bug).

panels.title: Landmine warnings
panels.description: Warnings on the flag that is live: applied, but probably not what was meant. For example, sticky cache larger than the Workflow thread pool, more pollers than slots (a Java poller reserves a slot before it polls), or 1 WFT poller (Java raises it to 2).

panels.title: Worker generations started (range)
panels.description: Each flag change that altered the Worker started a new WorkerFactory: Java cannot change a running Worker's options. Each swap starts with an EMPTY sticky cache, so every open Workflow replays once (measured: hit ratio 75% for one 10 s window, then 100%). Swaps are rate-limited (TUNING_MIN_SWAP_INTERVAL_S), so a flapping flag cannot thrash the cache.

panels.title: Effective settings (configured, not measured)
panels.description:
What the flag configured, after the SDK's own adjustments (WFT pollers 1 becomes 2).

ON JAVA <1.30 THIS IS THE ONLY POLLER COUNT YOU HAVE. There is no num_pollers metric before 1.30, and DescribeTaskQueue counts poller identities (one per process), not concurrent polls: measured, a Worker with 2 Activity pollers read 'pollers: 1'.

panels.title: Workflow Task schedule-to-start p95
panels.description:
How long a Workflow Task waited on the server for a poller. THE saturation signal, and the number the tuning has to move.

Go/Java emit SECONDS (_seconds suffix); TypeScript/Python/.NET emit milliseconds with no suffix and do not appear here.

JAVA HISTOGRAM CEILING: Micrometer's default timer histogram stops at 30 s (verified: a 120 s sample lands in +Inf), so beyond 30 s this panel flatlines at 30 s. The lab Worker raises it to 10 min with a MeterFilter; copy that into your Workers.

panels.title: Activity schedule-to-start p95
panels.description:
How long a Activity waited on the server for a poller. THE saturation signal, and the number the tuning has to move.

Go/Java emit SECONDS (_seconds suffix); TypeScript/Python/.NET emit milliseconds with no suffix and do not appear here.

JAVA HISTOGRAM CEILING: Micrometer's default timer histogram stops at 30 s (verified: a 120 s sample lands in +Inf), so beyond 30 s this panel flatlines at 30 s. The lab Worker raises it to 10 min with a MeterFilter; copy that into your Workers.

panels.title: Server backlog (sum across partitions)
panels.description:
The server's own backlog gauge, summed across partitions. Use the SERVER task queue variable: the server sanitises the name (lab-java becomes lab_java).

Cross-check against schedule-to-start, not alone: after a mass termination this gauge froze for minutes while the SDK measured 39 s waits.

panels.title: 3 · Slots: is the Worker allowed to take more?
Slots used / available
panels.description:
Available at 0 with CPU idle: slot-bound. Raise slots before adding Workers.

UNDER RESOURCE_BASED there is no ActivityWorker 'available' line: 1.28.4 does not report it with a tuner. That absence is correct. With a plain Micrometer reporter the line instead FREEZES at the last MANUAL value (measured: 10 shown, 1 actually granted). Read the tuner panel to the right instead.

panels.title: ResourceBasedTuner: what it sees
panels.description:
The tuner's inputs. Before SDK 1.32 these have NO temporal_ prefix (resource_slots_*). Both names are queried here.

CPU is getSystemCpuLoad(), the whole container or host, not this process, so a busy sidecar throttles your slots. Memory is JVM heap / -Xmx, garbage included, and blind to thread stacks and direct buffers.

Measured: with target 60% the tuner held CPU near 0.6 by granting 1-2 of 50 slots while schedule-to-start grew past 23 s. It caps resource use, not latency. It is not an autoscaler. Empty in MANUAL mode.

panels.title: 4 · Pollers: is the Worker asking often enough?
Pollers: measured (1.30+/Go) and configured (flag)
panels.description:
Measured comes from num_pollers, which needs Java SDK 1.30+. Configured comes from the flag.

Java SPLITS its WFT pollers between the sticky and normal queues, so configured 4 means 4 polls in total. Go polls sticky ADDITIONALLY, so the same number means more polls on Go.

panels.title: Poll latency p50 (long poll RPC)

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.5, sum by (le, operation) (rate(temporal_long_request_latency_seconds_bucket{job=~"$job", namespace=~"$namespace", task_queue=~"$task_queue|none", operation=~"Poll(Activity|Workflow)TaskQueue"}[$__rate_interval])))

panels.description:
THE discriminator between poller-bound and server-bound, measured on the lab. With a backlog waiting:
- polls return in 2-16 ms: the server had the task ready, and the Worker isn't asking often enough. Poller-bound, so raise pollers.
- polls take 0.6-1.0 s: the server is slow to hand work out. More pollers won't help; check row 7.

With NO backlog, a long poll waits by design, so ignore this panel when nothing is queued.

Go reports this metric with task_queue="none", so it is filtered by Fleet (job), not by queue.

panels.title: Sync match rate (server)
panels.description:
Share of tasks handed straight to a waiting poller. Near 100% means pollers are waiting for work, and the Worker is not short of pollers.

Hidden below 0.1 dispatches/s: an idle queue's ratio is noise. Async match is poll_success - poll_success_sync. poll_timeouts is NOT async match.

panels.title: 5 · Java Worker internals: cache, threads, JVM
Sticky cache: held vs configured, and Workflow threads
panels.description:
THE JAVA TRAP. Each cached Workflow parks a Workflow thread, so the cache can never hold more than maxWorkflowThreads - 1, whatever its configured size.

Measured: cache 1000, 20 threads: cached Workflows sat at 19, and 58% of Workflow Tasks missed and replayed, with slots free and CPU idle. Raising threads to 1000 took it to 40 cached (every open Workflow) and a 100% hit rate within 6 s.

Cached Workflows flat at threads - 1 while the configured cache is larger: raise threads, not the cache.

panels.title: Sticky cache hit ratio, and forced thread evictions
panels.description:
Hit ratio below about 80% means most Workflow Tasks replay history. Cheap on short histories (replay p95 under 1 ms here), expensive on long ones.

Thread-forced evictions UNDERSTATE the thread trap: measured 0.4/s while misses ran at 10/s. Most misses came from the capped cache, not from evictions, so judge by the left panel, not by this line.

Do NOT alert on temporal_sticky_cache_total_forced_eviction: it counts ordinary completions (measured 1:1 with completed Workflows).

panels.title: JVM: process CPU, heap, live threads

targets.expr: sum by (instance) (jvm_memory_used_bytes{job=~"$job", area="heap"}) / sum by (instance) (jvm_memory_max_bytes{job=~"$job", area="heap"} > 0)

panels.description:
Check CPU BEFORE pollers: a CPU-starved Worker looks poller-bound, because its pollers are starved too (measured on the Go lane).

Live threads: every busy Activity slot and every cached Workflow is a platform thread, with its stack OUTSIDE the heap. Size the container for threads × stack, not just -Xmx. During a flag swap both generations' threads exist together.

process_cpu_usage is a fraction of ALL cores visible to the JVM.

panels.title: 6 · Load generator (k6): was the load actually delivered?
Starts / s by step
panels.description:
Workflow starts the SERVER accepted, from demo/k6/worker-tuning (remote write). A step that doesn't reach its target rate is a test that didn't deliver its load: read nothing about Worker capacity from it.

Empty if k6 ran without `-o experimental-prometheus-rw`.

panels.title: Starts throttled / failed
panels.description: Throttled means a namespace RPS/APS limit (Cloud) or a frontend rate limit (self-hosted). The load never reached the Workers, so fix the limit first. k6 creates these counters on the first event, so 'throttled' falls back to 0 rather than No data.

panels.title: Start RPC latency (k6 view)
panels.description: StartWorkflowExecution as seen from the load generator, network included. It measures the server, NOT your Workers: starts stay fast while Workers fall arbitrarily behind. Worker capacity is row 2 and the k6 teardown count of Workflows still Running.

panels.title: 7 · Server: rule it out before tuning Workers
Persistence latency p95
panels.description:
Self-hosted only. Measured on the lab: 2.7-4.6 ms healthy, 96 ms with Postgres CPU-capped (make lab-slow-db). A slow server holds slots open until completion RPCs return, which reads as slot-bound. Check this BEFORE raising slots.

Server CPU alone is NOT evidence: at 240% server CPU the Workers were poller-bound, and the polls returned in 8-16 ms.

panels.title: Task completion RPC p95 (frontend)
panels.description: Measured: 32-48 ms healthy, 2-4 s server-bound. On Temporal Cloud, use the Cloud board instead: these are self-hosted server metrics.

list.label: Task queue (SDK)
list.name: task_queue
list.description: As the SDK labels it. Java keeps dashes (lab-java); Go sanitises them (lab_go).

list.label: Task queue (server)
list.name: server_task_queue
list.description: As the SERVER labels it: dashes become underscores (lab-java → lab_java). A separate variable on purpose: one variable joined across both matches nothing on one side.
